---
title: "Full tutorial: dating hybrid populations in five real datasets"
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5,
                      dpi = 110, cache = TRUE)
```

This tutorial runs hybridclock on the five example datasets that come with
the package. Each one is a different situation that people studying
hybrids run into: a captive cross with a known pedigree, an advanced
intercross with a genetic map, a closed population founded once, a genetic
rescue typed at microsatellites, and an invasive hybrid zone where only an
upper bound on age is known. In every case the true age of the hybrids is
known or bounded, so you can see how close the estimates come.

The settings follow the rules used to validate the package on 23 truth
sets (Maier, in review): describe what is known about the population, and
keep the ranges generous. To keep the run time down, each reference here
has 2,000 simulated histories. For real analyses use 6,000 or more. The
whole tutorial takes about 15 minutes on four cores; most of that is
building the references.

```{r packages}
library(hybridclock)
cores <- 4
```

## 1. Recent hybrids: Mexican wolves

The Mexican wolf (*Canis lupus baileyi*) was saved from extinction by three
captive lineages, which were kept apart for 15 to 20 years and then crossed.
The `wolves` data hold pure wolves of two lineages, McBride (`ref1`) and
Ghost Ranch (`ref2`), and the F1s, first backcrosses and second backcrosses
that followed, each with its class from the studbook.

First, choose diagnostic markers from the two reference groups and score
every wolf. The hybrid index *S* is the share of alleles from species 2
(here Ghost Ranch), and the interspecies heterozygosity *H* is the share of
markers with one allele from each.

```{r wolves-scores}
mk <- diagnostic_markers(wolves$genotypes, wolves$groups, "ref1", "ref2")
nrow(mk)
sc <- hybrid_scores(wolves$genotypes, mk)
plot_triangle(sc, wolves$groups)
```

The F1s sit at the top of the triangle (*S* = 0.5, *H* = 1), and each
backcross halves *H* and moves toward the McBride corner. With 486 markers,
individual classes are easy:

```{r wolves-classes}
cl <- classify_hybrids(sc)
table(studbook = wolves$animals$class, called = cl$class)
```

Every wolf is placed in its studbook class. To date the hybrids as a
population, build a reference of simulated histories that matches the data
(the number of markers, the sample size, and a genetic map given as a
number of chromosomes and a range of total lengths), train the clock, and
estimate:

```{r wolves-clock}
hyb <- !wolves$groups %in% c("ref1", "ref2")
ref <- build_reference(n_sims = 2000, generations = 20, n_markers = nrow(mk),
                       sample_size = sum(hyb), het_dropout = c(0, 0),
                       map = list(chromosomes = c(38, 38), length_cM = c(1800, 2400)),
                       cores = cores, seed = 1)
clock <- train_clock(ref, cores = cores)
diag <- orient_genotypes(wolves$genotypes, mk)
est <- estimate_history(clock, sc[hyb, ], rep("hybrids", sum(hyb)), diag = diag[hyb, ])
est[, c("population", "n_hybrids", "method", "hybrid_age_both",
        "hybrid_age_both_lower", "hybrid_age_both_upper", "information")]
mean(wolves$animals$hybrid_age[hyb])
```

Every hybrid fits an early class, so the answer comes from the individual
classes (`method`), and it matches the true mean age from the studbook.

## 2. An advanced intercross with a genetic map: chickens

The `chickens` data are generation F8 of an intercross between Red
Junglefowl and White Leghorn chickens, kept as a closed line of about 100
birds. Every bird is eight generations from the pure parents. Individual
classes cannot tell an F8 from an F2:

```{r chickens-classes}
g <- chickens$genotypes
mkc <- data.frame(column = seq_len(ncol(g)), name = colnames(g), flip = FALSE,
                  freq1 = 0, freq2 = 1)
scc <- hybrid_scores(g, mkc)
table(classify_hybrids(scc)$class)
```

The population clock can. Here the breeding design is documented, so the
reference uses it: F1 founders, a closed line with no sibling mating, one
breeding group and random mating. The genetic map is known, and with a map
the clock also uses ancestry switches between neighboring markers, which
multiply with every generation of recombination. A map is never exact, so
its length is stretched or shrunk by up to 25% in each history
(`map_scale`). Leaving that out makes the intervals too narrow.

```{r chickens-clock}
pos <- chickens$map[, c("chromosome", "position")]
refc <- build_reference(n_sims = 2000, generations = 50, breeders = c(30, 150),
                        n_markers = nrow(mkc), sample_size = 20,
                        founders = "F1", kinds = c(closed = 1, one = 0, both = 0),
                        sib_mating = c(0, 0), pools = 1, assort = c(0, 0),
                        het_dropout = c(0, 0), map = pos, map_scale = c(0.75, 1.25),
                        cores = cores, seed = 2)
clockc <- train_clock(refc, cores = cores)
estc <- estimate_history(clockc, scc, chickens$groups, diag = g, positions = pos,
                         repeats = 20)
estc[, c("population", "n", "method", "hybrid_age_both",
         "hybrid_age_both_lower", "hybrid_age_both_upper")]
```

The true age is 8. The warning says that every simulated history here has
no backcrosses and no arrivals, so those quantities are not estimated. A
known map roughly halves the width of the intervals
compared with a map given only as a range of lengths.

## 3. A single founding of a closed population: burrowing bettongs

Burrowing bettongs (*Bettongia lesueur*) from two subspecies were released
together into a fenced reserve in 2010 and sampled every year until 2018.
No new animals arrived, so the population is closed. Bettongs can breed in
their first year, so the hybrids sampled *k* years after the release can be
at most *k* generations old.

These genotypes have heterozygote dropout: about a quarter of heterozygotes
are called homozygous. The classifier needs to know this, and the
settings given to `class_settings()` are stored with the reference, so the
simulated and the real samples are classified the same way.

```{r bettongs}
mkb <- diagnostic_markers(bettongs$genotypes, bettongs$groups, "ref1", "ref2")
scb <- hybrid_scores(bettongs$genotypes, mkb)
diagb <- orient_genotypes(bettongs$genotypes, mkb)
years <- bettongs$truth$group[bettongs$truth$n >= 15 & !is.na(bettongs$truth$year)]
keep <- bettongs$groups %in% years
refb <- build_reference(n_sims = 2000, generations = 10, n_markers = nrow(mkb),
                        sample_size = 15, kinds = c(closed = 1, one = 0, both = 0),
                        het_dropout = c(0.15, 0.35),
                        map = list(chromosomes = c(10, 12), length_cM = c(800, 2000)),
                        missing = rowMeans(is.na(diagb[keep, ])),
                        class_settings = class_settings(het_dropout = 0.25),
                        cores = cores, seed = 3)
clockb <- train_clock(refb, cores = cores)
estb <- estimate_history(clockb, scb[keep, ], bettongs$groups[keep], diag = diagb[keep, ])
data.frame(estb[, c("population", "n_hybrids", "method", "hybrid_age_both",
                    "hybrid_age_both_lower", "hybrid_age_both_upper")],
           bound = bettongs$truth$max_hybrid_age[match(estb$population, bettongs$truth$group)])
```

From 2012 on, hybrid age stays at about two generations while the time
since the release grows, which fits a generation time of about three years:
the reserve had seen fewer than three generations by 2018
(`bettongs$truth$generations_at_3yr`). The 2011 sample has only three
hybrids, and its estimate is above the bound of one generation. A
population estimate from so few hybrids should not be trusted.

## 4. Microsatellites: a genetic rescue of mountain pygmy possums

The mountain pygmy possum (*Burramys parvus*) population at Mount Buller
was rescued in 2011 by releasing six males from Mount Higginbotham. The
`possums` data hold 24 microsatellites. Microsatellites rarely have alleles
fixed between species, so *S* and *H* are estimated by likelihood from the
reference allele frequencies, and the reference simulates alleles drawn from
those frequencies.

```{r possums}
ms <- microsat_markers(possums$alleles, possums$groups, "ref1", "ref2")
scp <- hybrid_scores_microsat(possums$alleles, ms)
yrs <- c("Buller2012", "Buller2013", "Buller2014", "Buller2015")
keep <- possums$groups %in% yrs
refp <- build_reference(n_sims = 2000, generations = 10, sample_size = 20,
                        microsat = ms, het_dropout = c(0, 0), cores = cores, seed = 4)
clockp <- train_clock(refp, cores = cores)
estp <- estimate_history(clockp, scp[keep, ], possums$groups[keep])
estp[, c("population", "n_hybrids", "method", "hybrid_age_both",
         "hybrid_age_both_lower", "hybrid_age_both_upper")]
possums$truth[possums$truth$group %in% yrs, c("group", "hybrid_age")]
```

The 2012 hybrids are all F1s (age 1), and those of 2013 are F1s, F2s and
backcrosses (about 1.5). In 2014 and 2015 only upper bounds are known: 3
and 4 generations.

## 5. An invasive hybrid zone with generic settings: Asian carp

Bighead and silver carp were imported from China in 1973, were in the open
waters of the Mississippi River basin by the early 1980s, and have
hybridized there since. The `carp` data hold three
river sites sampled in 2009 to 2011. Only an upper bound on hybrid age is
known: about 12 generations, from the time since the imports and a
generation time of at least three years. Little
is known about the breeding population, so the reference uses the package
defaults: up to 50 generations, 10 to 500 breeders, any founding share, and
arrivals of either species allowed. The map is given as the carp karyotype
(24 chromosomes) and a broad range of lengths.

```{r carp}
mkk <- diagnostic_markers(carp$genotypes, carp$groups, "ref1", "ref2")
sck <- hybrid_scores(carp$genotypes, mkk)
diagk <- orient_genotypes(carp$genotypes, mkk)
sites <- c("IMAR", "PL26", "MKY")
keep <- carp$groups %in% sites
refk <- build_reference(n_sims = 2000, n_markers = nrow(mkk), sample_size = 20,
                        het_dropout = c(0, 0),
                        map = list(chromosomes = c(24, 24), length_cM = c(1500, 3500)),
                        cores = cores, seed = 5)
clockk <- train_clock(refk, cores = cores)
estk <- estimate_history(clockk, sck[keep, ], carp$groups[keep], diag = diagk[keep, ],
                         repeats = 20)
estk[, c("population", "n_hybrids", "method", "hybrid_age_both",
         "hybrid_age_both_lower", "hybrid_age_both_upper", "arriving", "information")]
```

All three sites are below the bound of 12 generations. The lower Mississippi
site (`MKY`) has the fewest hybrids and the widest interval, and its lower
`information` value says that much of its answer reflects the reference's
range. The probability that pure fish are still arriving is between about
one third and two thirds; F1s born as late as 2006 show that hybridization
was still going on.

## Reading the answer

Each row of `estimate_history()` is one population. The columns to read
first are:

- `method`: `"individual classes"` when the answer comes from the classes
  (samples made up of F1s and backcrosses, where the reference shows the
  classes to be more accurate), `"population clock"` otherwise.
- `hybrid_age_both` with `_lower` and `_upper`: the hybrid age and its 90%
  interval. Hybrid age is the number of generations back to the nearest pure
  ancestor, averaged over the lines of each hybrid's pedigree and then over
  the hybrids.
- `hybrid_age_rare` and `backcrosses`: how long ago the rarer species' genes
  entered, and how many matings with pure animals there have been since the
  first cross.
- `arriving`: the probability that pure animals of the rarer species are
  still arriving. When they are, hybrid age levels off, and it is then a
  lower bound on the time since contact.
- `information`: near 1 when the interval is much narrower than the range
  of the reference, near 0 when the answer mostly reflects the settings.
  Low values usually mean few or weak markers.

## Using your own data

The same steps apply to any pair of species or lineages:

1. Choose diagnostic markers with `diagnostic_markers()` from pure reference
   samples, or `microsat_markers()` for microsatellites. For SNPs that are
   not fixed, give the reference allele frequencies to `build_reference()`
   (`freq`); see the vignette.
2. Check that the markers are diagnostic in the animals that actually bred,
   with `check_markers()`, if your sample has F1s.
3. Build a reference that describes what you know, with generous ranges:
   the founders (`founders`), whether the population is closed (`kinds`),
   a ceiling on the number of generations from the earliest possible date
   of contact (`generations`), the breeding size (`breeders`), and the map.
4. Train the clock and estimate, and read the `information` column.

`markers_needed()` helps plan a study: dating F2 families within half a
generation took about 50 diagnostic markers in simulations, and older
populations need more.

## Citation

If you use hybridclock, please cite both:

- Maier PA, Mabe JA, Hale JL, Herman AE, Kantz BP (2024) Hybridization
  between *Anaxyrus boreas* × *canorus* within Eldorado National Forest:
  the first genomic assessment. Final report to the US Forest Service.
- Maier PA (2026) hybridclock: Dating hybrid populations beyond F2, with or
  without a genetic map. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*, in review.

Run `citation("hybridclock")` for the entries.

The example data come from Fitak et al. (2018, *Journal of Heredity*),
Johnsson et al. (2016, *Genetics*), Rick et al. (2019, *Genes*), Weeks et
al. (2017, *Nature Communications*) and Lamer et al. (2015, *Molecular
Ecology*); see the help page of each dataset for the full references and
licences.
